stories.why: Japan sits on the "Ring of Fire" and records roughly a fifth of the world's earthquakes, but a shallow M7.1 directly under a populated region is at the severe end and the tsunami and landslide risk will keep the response tense for days.

stories.headline: DeepSeek's MLA splits content from position
stories.summary: Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) — the attention variant introduced in DeepSeek-V2 that squeezes the key-value cache through a shared low-rank bottleneck (a compression step that cuts memory ~81% at inference, the main cost of long context) — is now in production models, but nobody had checked what the bottleneck keeps and what it throws away. Training a small 114M-parameter transformer end to end and probing its internals, the authors find the compressed channel learns an almost pure content representation: it retains entity identity (98%) while discarding positional information, which the model reconstructs elsewhere.
stories.why: MLA is one of the load-bearing tricks behind cheap long context, copied into models most people now use, yet it was adopted for its memory savings without anyone knowing what it costs representationally. A clean it separates content from position, and here's where position goes is exactly the kind of grounding that lets the next architecture tweak be deliberate rather than superstitious. That the study runs at 114M rather than frontier scale is the honest caveat.
stories.affiliation_label: IIT Madras, P P Savani University

stories.headline: Netanyahu and Zelenskyy meet Trump
stories.summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy both descended on Washington on Tuesday 28 July to meet President Donald Trump, as a long-stalled Russia-sanctions bill neared a Senate vote and the wars in Iran and Ukraine visibly converged. Both leaders were in the US chiefly for the funeral of Senator Lindsey Graham, a Trump ally and hawkish backer of both Israel and Ukraine who died on 11 July; Netanyahu was set to meet Trump with the US-Israel war on Iran topping the agenda, while Zelenskyy pressed for anti-ballistic-missile defences and help producing Patriot systems. The sanctions bill Graham championed would impose 100% tariffs on the five largest buyers of Russian oil and gas - including China and India - and Trump has moved at the last minute to fold sanctions on Iran into the same package. The convergence is concrete: Ukraine attacked an Iranian tanker in the Caspian Sea on Saturday 25 July that it says was ferrying drones and components to Russia, Iran has vowed to retaliate, and Russia said more than 390 Ukrainian drones struck the Moscow region overnight. Trump has said talks with Iran are under way during the current pause in US strikes.
stories.why: Two wars 2,500 km apart are being wired together through Washington's sanctions machinery and Iran's arms pipeline to Moscow - treat both leaders' framing as advocacy, since each is seeking Trump's backing.

stories.headline: Wildfires push 300,000 from homes near Bordeaux
stories.summary: Wildfires around Bordeaux drove one of the largest evacuations in French history, with around 300,000 people now moved to safety across France and Spain and the flames roughly 15 km from the city. In southwest France the fire in the Gironde has burned more than 19,000 hectares and destroyed about 100 buildings since Wednesday, forcing some 220,000 people from their homes — 55,000 more ordered out around Bordeaux over the weekend, and 31,000 in neighbouring Landes; boats were used to evacuate holidaymakers from the Cap Ferret peninsula. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said the blaze turned "extremely violent and unpredictable" overnight, the A63 motorway to Spain is shut over about 60 km, and nearly 100,000 hectares have burned nationwide since January — a historic record. In Spain the government declared a state of emergency around Madrid and in Ávila (where about 47,000 hectares burned), with roughly 90,000 people evacuated according to the interior ministry; El País reports the Madrid, Ávila and Toledo fires have covered some 77,000 hectares in all. A new heatwave with temperatures up to 40°C is forecast from Tuesday 28 July, threatening to worsen the fight.
stories.why: This is the sharp escalation of a fire emergency running across France, Spain and Italy since 23 July — the direct threat to Bordeaux, a metropolis of about 850,000, and the incoming heat push it well beyond the earlier evacuations.

stories.headline: Pogacar equals all-time Tour record
stories.summary: Slovenia's Tadej Pogacar (UAE Team Emirates-XRG) sealed his fifth Tour de France on the Champs-Elysees, drawing level with the sport's four all-time greats - Jacques Anquetil, Eddy Merckx, Bernard Hinault and Miguel Indurain - as the only riders to win cycling's biggest race five times. It is his third in a row. As flagged here last week, the contest had effectively closed once his one real threat, two-time winner Jonas Vingegaard, abandoned with a broken collarbone on stage 15; his other rival, Belgium's Remco Evenepoel, finished second overall, 6 minutes 26 seconds back. Pogacar, 27, took five stage wins including a record ascent of Alpe d'Huez.
stories.why: Five wins puts Pogacar in the conversation as the greatest cyclist ever - but the reception is telling. He was booed by some fans during the race, less out of dislike than frustration that his dominance has drained the Tour of suspense. That tension - a generational champion whose brilliance makes the event less competitive - is now the sport's central question.

stories.headline: Iran vows retaliation over Caspian Sea strike
stories.summary: Iran warned Ukraine it will retaliate for a deadly strike on an Iranian commercial vessel in the Caspian Sea, opening a new front that links the Russia–Ukraine war to the recent US–Israel conflict with Iran. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday 26 July that the Ukrainian attack the day before — which Iran says caused the ship to explode, killing one sailor and injuring several — "cannot go unanswered" and violated the UN Charter, and he accused Israel of provoking it to "drag Europe into its war." Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his forces had hit "vessels used in military cargo shipments involving Iran, as well as a warship" in long-range strikes, and accused Russia of feeding Iran satellite imagery of US facilities in the Gulf. Iran has summoned Ukraine's chargé d'affaires in Tehran, and a senior lawmaker said early Monday that Kyiv "may soon come to understand that Iran does not let actions go unanswered." Separately, the United States and Iran held off on fresh strikes for a second straight day, and oil prices eased.
stories.why: Kyiv striking an Iranian ship — over Tehran's supply of Shahed drones to Moscow since 2022 — risks pulling Iran directly into the Ukraine war just as a fragile pause in the US–Iran fighting takes hold.

stories.headline: Swiss Super League season opens
stories.summary: The 2026-27 Swiss Super League - the country's twelve-team top flight - kicked off this weekend, and the two marquee Sunday fixtures both turned on late comebacks. In front of a sold-out St. Gallen, the hosts trailed to a first-half Umeh Emmanuel goal for Zurich before Lukas Goertler equalised from a worked corner (70') and summer signing Andrin Hunziker deflected in the winner four minutes later for a 2-1 St. Gallen victory. It was a pointed result for FCZ's new coach Marcel Koller - the man who led St. Gallen to their last league title 26 years ago - whose reshaped side created the better first-half chances but left empty-handed. In Bern, Young Boys threw away a 2-0 lead against Sion before Samuel Essende's second-half brace rescued a 4-2 win.
stories.why: For most Swiss towns the Super League - not the World Cup that just finished - is the sport that structures the autumn, and the opening weekend already hints at the season's shape: a champion (Thun) nobody expected to defend, a rebuilt Zurich under a returning veteran coach, and a St. Gallen side punching above its weight at home and in Europe.

stories.headline: Van hits Berlin Pride crowd, one killed
stories.summary: A van drove into a crowd at Berlin's Christopher Street Day (the city's Pride march) late on Saturday 25 July, killing one person and injuring 16, three of them life-threateningly. The vehicle, a white transporter, struck marchers around 22:00 near Potsdamer Platz in the Tiergarten, and the parade was called off. Berlin police say they identified a fleeing suspect overnight — a 21-year-old man reported by German outlets as Abdul B. — and a citywide manhunt is under way; police describe him as having links to what they call the "Islamist scene," a characterisation that comes from investigators and has not been confirmed by any court or established motive. Of the injured, eight are seriously and five lightly hurt.
stories.why: It is the latest in a run of deadly vehicle-ramming attacks in Germany, and both the target — a Pride event — and the still-unproven motive will shape a charged domestic debate over security and extremism; treat the early "Islamist" framing as a police working theory, not a settled fact.

stories.headline: Swiss cantons ban 1 August fireworks
stories.summary: Several Swiss cantons have issued explicit fireworks bans for the 1 August national holiday as a weeks-long drought keeps most of the country under open-fire restrictions. With near-total bans on open fires already in place across much of Switzerland — Zürich and Winterthur, for instance, prohibit even charcoal grilling in public — cantons have in recent days tightened the rules specifically for fireworks ahead of Saturday 1 August, meaning the traditional displays will be barred almost everywhere.
stories.why: It is a concrete, everyday sign of the same European heat-and-drought spell driving the wildfires abroad, and it reshapes how the country's biggest civic holiday will be marked this year.

stories.headline: Saudi-led coalition strikes Hodeida as Houthis vow response, widening the Gulf war
stories.summary: A Saudi-led coalition struck the Houthi-held Yemeni port of Hodeida on Friday 24 July, and the Iran-backed Houthis vowed to retaliate on Saturday 25 July, pulling Saudi Arabia directly into the widening Gulf war. The strikes followed several days of Houthi attacks on Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea; Riyadh said it hit military targets and would "do everything necessary" to protect its shipping against a Houthi-enforced maritime blockade, while the Houthis said the strikes hit civilian infrastructure in Hodeida and injured two people. The flare-up opens a new front alongside the ongoing US-Iran confrontation over the Strait of Hormuz, and the UN warned on 24 July against a wider escalation as fighting intensified around the Red Sea, a corridor that normally carries a large share of world seaborne trade.
stories.why: A direct Saudi-Houthi exchange layered on top of the US-Iran war threatens both of the region's two critical maritime chokepoints (Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb) at once, and any sustained closure of Red Sea shipping feeds straight into global energy and freight costs.

stories.headline: Three detectors, one ultra-high-energy neutrino puzzle they can't reconcile
stories.summary: Ultra-high-energy neutrinos are the most energetic particles known, and three very different instruments have now seen events that don't add up. The balloon experiment ANITA-IV recorded four steep, near-horizon events that look like such neutrinos, and the underwater telescope KM3NeT logged a single record-breaking track — but both imply neutrino rates that IceCube, the largest detector of all, should have seen and did not. The authors build careful energy- and direction-dependent sensitivities for all three and do a joint statistical fit. A steady all-sky neutrino flux fails badly, leaving a ~7.5-sigma tension (sigma measures how many standard deviations the data sit from the model; 5-sigma is the particle-physics discovery threshold, so 7.5-sigma is a serious mismatch); even short transient flares tuned to the observation windows only ease it to ~5.9-sigma. Within the Standard Model, no arrangement of ordinary astrophysical sources reconciles the three datasets.
stories.why: a genuine, high-significance puzzle at the energy frontier that points either to new physics or to something the field doesn't yet understand about its own detectors — the kind of anomaly that occasionally reshapes a subfield.

stories.headline: Custom RNA drugs cut seizures in two children with a rare genetic epilepsy
stories.summary: Two boys, aged 9 and 14, with SCN2A-related developmental and epileptic encephalopathy each received a bespoke antisense oligonucleotide (ASO — a short synthetic genetic strand designed to stick to a chosen RNA and silence it). Each drug was engineered to knock down only the mutated copy of the SCN2A sodium-channel gene while sparing the healthy copy, by targeting single-letter DNA differences unique to the bad allele. Seizures fell by 26% and 90% respectively, medication dropped, neurodevelopment improved, and one child walked independently for the first time — with no drug-related serious adverse events. This is an n-of-1-times-two result, so it is preliminary and needs long follow-up, but the team showed that 16% of a separate SCN2A infant cohort carry differences compatible with the same approach.
stories.why: a concrete demonstration that truly individualized genetic medicines can be built and deployed for ultra-rare mutations — with an early hint of how to move from n=1 toward many.
affiliations: Rady Children's Institute for Genomic Medicine
stories.affiliation_label: UC San Diego, Rady Children's Institute for Genomic Medicine

stories.headline: Europe wildfires force 200,000 from homes across France, Spain and Italy
stories.summary: Wildfires across western France, central Spain and Italy have now forced roughly 200,000 people from their homes, authorities said Saturday 25 July, as separate blazes merged and hot, dry, windy conditions kept them out of control. In France's Gironde and Landes departments the fire drove mass evacuations around Bordeaux, while Spain - which declared its first-ever national wildfire emergency on Thursday 23 July over blazes near Madrid and in Avila - and Italy continued to battle major fires amid a Europe-wide heatwave. DW reported conditions that made it "nearly impossible for firefighters to gain the upper hand."
stories.why: The evacuation total has roughly quadrupled in two days, marking one of the worst fire seasons on record for southern Europe and straining cross-border firefighting resources at peak summer.

stories.headline: AMD and Anthropic strike a deal to deploy up to 2 gigawatts of MI450 GPUs for Claude
stories.summary: AMD and Anthropic announced a strategic partnership under which Anthropic will deploy up to 2 gigawatts of AMD's MI450-series GPUs to train and run its Claude models. The Decoder reports the arrangement is worth up to $5 billion in AMD investment; it follows comparable AMD deals with Meta and OpenAI as the company presses its challenge to Nvidia's near-monopoly on AI accelerators. This confirms the AMD second-sourcing signal flagged as unverified in the 2026-07-21 edition — where an Anthropic move to AMD was inferred from indirect signals — with a named, on-the-record partnership.
stories.why: Nvidia's dominance of training and inference silicon is the single biggest cost and supply chokepoint in the industry, and credible second-sourcing by the largest model builders is what actually erodes its pricing power over time. Anthropic committing at 2-gigawatt scale is a concrete data point that the challenge is real, not aspirational — though the "up to" framing on both the power and the dollar figure leaves the realized size open.

stories.headline: US hits Switzerland with 12.5% tariff over forced-labour claims
stories.summary: The US slapped a new 12.5% tariff on Swiss goods from 06:01 Swiss time on Friday 24 July, the top rate in a forced-labour trade action hitting 60 economies. The US Trade Representative, Jamieson Greer, took "final action" under Section 301 of the 1974 Trade Act — the same durable legal tool Trump used against China in his first term — imposing 10% on partners that pledged to enforce a ban on imports made with forced labour and 12.5% on those USTR judged to have "failed to adopt" such a ban; Switzerland drew the higher rate. The levies took effect at 12:01am Washington time (04:01 GMT), the moment the temporary 10% worldwide tariff — a 150-day Section 122 stopgap adopted after the Supreme Court struck down Trump's broader IEEPA tariffs in February — expired. Swiss business reaction was immediate and hostile, with employers' groups quoted calling the move "unjustified and incomprehensible," and SRF noting Switzerland comes off worse than the EU, whose separate July trade deal caps most goods at a 15% all-inclusive ceiling.
stories.why: It lands a fresh, above-EU cost on Swiss exporters — pharma, machinery, watches — just as the prior tariff truce lapses, and reframes a US trade dispute as a human-rights enforcement claim against Swiss supply chains that Bern rejects.

stories.headline: A dense per-step reward built to help long-horizon agents instead collapses them into a do-nothing loop
stories.summary: A common recipe for teaching an agent to act over many steps is to hand it a small reward at every step for correctly predicting what it will observe next, on the theory that useful memory follows. Trained with GRPO (group-relative policy optimization — a popular RL method that scores each attempt against the average of a batch of attempts), the paper shows this recipe does not merely underperform: across Qwen3 models of three sizes on the ALFWorld household-task benchmark, it drives every run into a "dark room" — the agent maximizes prediction accuracy by doing nothing, task success falls to zero, and episodes run out the clock. A single-factor ablation pins the cause: removing only GRPO's step of dividing rewards by their standard deviation turns the same reward from catastrophic back to baseline. When every attempt in a batch fails, that division makes a bounded reward act as unbounded pressure toward the degenerate solution.
stories.why: dense reward-shaping is one of the obvious levers people reach for when sparse rewards make long-horizon agents hard to train, and this is a clean, mechanistic warning that a widely used normalization step can silently convert a helpful signal into a self-inflicted collapse. The fix is two lines of code, but the lesson — that the optimizer, not the environment, built the trap — is the useful part.

stories.headline: Swiss transport regulator orders cash and paper-ticket options preserved
stories.summary: The Federal Office of Transport (BAV) told Switzerland's public-transport operators on Friday 24 July that they must guarantee analogue, cash-payable ticket options as machines and cash acceptance disappear. In a written directive to the industry, the BAV said every transport company must ensure that people who cannot or do not want to buy tickets digitally still have a way to obtain a valid one; spokesperson Andreas Windlinger said such passengers "should not be left behind." The rules are binding. The industry body Alliance SwissPass defended its digitalisation drive but said it would comply, pointing to existing options such as loading a ticket onto a SwissPass by phone in some regions.
stories.why: It is a concrete federal check on the cashless push in daily Swiss life, protecting older passengers and those without smartphones from being locked out of the transport network.

board.headline: Houthi attacks kill dozens of Yemeni troops
board.summary: Houthi missile-and-drone assaults on Yemeni government camps killed at least 30 soldiers on Thursday 6 August 2026, the deadliest escalation since the 2022 truce. The Iran-backed Houthi movement struck military camps in the provinces of Marib and Hadramout, wounding around 50 more, according to Yemeni government officials; pro-government military sources put the toll higher, at 45 or above, and the Houthi spokesman claimed 'hundreds' of casualties — a figure that could not be independently verified. A de facto ceasefire between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition that backs Yemen's internationally recognised government has largely frozen the fighting since April 2022 without any formal peace deal; officials called these coordinated strikes the most serious breach in years.
board.why: A collapse of the truce would reopen a war that had faded from view and risks drawing the Saudi-led coalition — and, indirectly, the broader Iran-US confrontation — back into open conflict.

board.headline: Code beats JSON for LLM tool calls
board.summary: An LLM "agent" acts on the world by calling external tools. The usual method exposes each tool as a rigid JSON form the model fills in. This paper instead exposes tools as typed Python function stubs the model invokes by writing a short script — so it can chain and parallelize several calls in one turn (they call this programmatic tool calling, PTC). They run both head-to-head on BFCL v4 (the Berkeley Function-Calling Leaderboard, a standard tool-use benchmark) across 14 models. PTC matches or beats native JSON calling in 11 of 14 models — the GPT-5.6 family gains 10.6% — matches or wins in 13 of 14 under parallel "fan-out," and stays stable under "context rot" (long, cluttered conversations) where the JSON baseline slips ~2.3%.
board.why: As agents take on more multi-step work, how you let them call tools is a real performance lever, not an implementation detail. The result — with its nod to Sutton's "bitter lesson" that general, compute-scaling methods win — says the code-native path improves as models get more capable, while the JSON path does not.

board.headline: An optimal agnostic PAC learner
board.summary: PAC learning (Probably Approximately Correct — the standard theoretical model of supervised learning) asks how many labelled examples you need to come close to the best classifier in a given family. In the harder "agnostic" setting — where you do not assume the data can be perfectly separated — a lower bound on the achievable error has been known since the 1990s, but no algorithm had been proven to match it. This paper constructs a learner whose error is provably within a single universal constant of that lower bound, for any hypothesis family of finite VC dimension (VC dimension — a standard measure of a model family's capacity).
board.why: It settles a long-standing open question in learning theory — the sample complexity of agnostic PAC learning is now pinned down up to constants at every noise level. This is foundational rather than a product; the payoff is conceptual clarity about the fundamental limits of learning from data.

board.headline: Self-evolving agents poison their own skills
board.summary: "Self-evolving" agents get better by distilling reusable skills from their own past runs into a growing library. This paper shows the process is not monotonic: past a critical library size, newly added skills start hurting performance. The cause is structural — once a defective skill enters the decision context it becomes reference material for distilling later skills, forming cross-round contamination chains — and it is largely irreversible: deleting the original culprit afterward recovers only a small fraction of the lost performance. Their fix, Verifier-as-Gatekeeper (VaG), screens each candidate skill with three complementary critics (structural validity, behavioral harmlessness, semantic consistency) before admission. On Terminal-Bench 2, unfiltered accumulation peaks and then decays, while VaG improves every round to 72% pass@1 with a library roughly 5x smaller, and its frozen skill set transfers to other backbones.
board.why: It is a sharp warning for the popular "just let the agent keep learning from itself" design — quality control on what enters the skill memory has to be a pre-commit gate, because by the time a bad skill's damage shows up, cleaning it out no longer undoes the harm.

board.headline: Netanyahu reworks Gaza disarmament deal
board.summary: Israel has rewritten the Gaza disarmament roadmap it signed onto days earlier, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on 5 August 2026 that Israel had 'not agreed' to withdraw before Hamas is 'completely disarmed'. Under the Board of Peace framework that US President Donald Trump announced on 30 July — the multinational body (Egypt, Qatar, Turkey and the US) overseeing the ceasefire — Hamas was to surrender its weapons in stages while Israeli forces pulled back to the agreed 'Yellow Line'; Hamas accepted that version. Le Temps reports that Israeli-imposed modifications have since decoupled Hamas's disarmament from a full Israeli withdrawal, a change Hamas says voids its participation unless Israel meets its own obligations first. The characterisation of the reworked terms is contested — Israel presents them as clarifications, mediators and Hamas as a reversal of what was agreed.
board.why: A just-announced deal is being renegotiated before implementation, leaving the ceasefire's next phase in doubt.

board.headline: Teen gunman kills five at Thai school
board.summary: A teenage gunman killed five people at a school on the outskirts of Bangkok on Friday 7 August 2026 after fatally shooting his grandparents at home. Police said the suspect — a student enrolled at Debsirin Nonthaburi School in Nonthaburi province — opened fire with his grandfather's handgun, firing at least 26 rounds and carrying 34 more; at least 23 people were wounded, several critically. The attacker was also killed. Authorities initially reported six dead before revising the toll to five.
board.why: Mass shootings remain rare in Thailand relative to firearm-related violence overall, and a school attack by a minor will renew scrutiny of gun access in a country with high civilian ownership.

board.headline: Meta ordered to pay $567m in New Mexico
board.summary: A New Mexico judge ruled Meta a 'public nuisance' and ordered it to pay $567 million over harms its apps cause to children, in a decision issued late Thursday 6 August 2026. Judge Bryan Biedscheid in Santa Fe sided with the state, directing that $420 million of the sum fund treatment services for young people and the rest go to prevention and screening over five years; the award is on top of $375 million in civil penalties a jury imposed in March. The ruling also orders Meta to block New Mexico teens' access to its apps during school hours and overnight, set their accounts to private by default, and bar minors from 'romantic or sexualised' exchanges with its AI chatbots. Meta said it disagrees and will appeal.
board.why: It is one of the largest state-level penalties yet tying a social-media platform's design to child-safety harms, and its behavioural mandates could become a template other states copy.

board.headline: Turkey sends PKK disarmament law to parliament
board.summary: Turkey submitted a long-awaited framework law to parliament on Wednesday 5 August 2026 setting the legal basis to disarm the outlawed Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK). The bill governs how PKK fighters lay down arms and the judicial handling of people linked to the group, and its imprisoned founder Abdullah Ocalan has reportedly signed off on the current draft. The government hopes to pass it before parliament's summer recess. Disputes remain: the PKK wants legal reforms on prosecutions and Kurdish political participation to accompany disarmament, while Ankara insists the group disarm fully first.
board.why: It is the most concrete legislative step yet in a peace process that could end one of the region's longest insurgencies, running since 1984.

board.headline: Dittli fights back with legal opinion
board.summary: Vaud state councillor Valerie Dittli went on the offensive on Friday 7 August 2026, releasing a legal opinion that finds her right to be heard was 'gravely violated' during the cantonal government's handling of the Meylan report. The report, published on 24 April 2026, alleged that Dittli had secured a mandate and paid 10,000 francs of public money to the former head of a commission on agricultural land, who in return dropped a criminal complaint; a prosecutor opened a criminal investigation on the basis of it. Two constitutional-law experts commissioned by Dittli concluded the administrative-procedure guarantees were breached — deadlines too short, insufficient opportunity to respond — and Dittli, in a personal statement, called what she experienced 'extremely serious.'
board.why: The dispute over process, not just the underlying allegations, now shadows the Vaud executive and could bear on the criminal case against a sitting cantonal minister.

board.headline: Exact closed-form Muon on Stiefel manifold
board.summary: Muon is a recent "matrix-aware" optimizer — it treats a weight matrix as a matrix rather than a flat list of numbers — that has drawn attention for training large models efficiently. Many problems need weights whose columns are orthonormal, i.e. points on the Stiefel manifold (the set of matrices with orthonormal columns, ubiquitous in ML and scientific computing). Existing ways to run Muon on that manifold relied on approximate or iterative inner steps. This paper shows the corresponding update has an exact closed-form solution and packages it as Skewon, a practical algorithm for orthogonality-constrained optimization, with first-order convergence guarantees in the smooth non-convex setting.
board.why: Optimizers are where a lot of quiet training efficiency lives, and this is a distinct advance in the active Muon line (the last edition covered a separate Muon-for-diffusion fix): an exact, cheap update means practitioners can enforce orthogonality without paying for an inner solver each step.

board.headline: Markov-chain routing of transformer layers
board.summary: Standard LLMs run their layers once, in order. "Layer routing" asks whether a different path — skipping some layers, repeating others — does better on a given task. Prior methods needed weight updates, an expensive per-example search, or ground-truth labels at inference. MACRO (Markov Chain Routing) instead learns the route as a Markov policy — a probabilistic rule that picks the next move based only on the current state — over skip, repeat and residual-add operations, leaving the model's weights untouched, then decodes high-probability routes with a top-k Viterbi search. It reports +5.0% average accuracy over unrouted baselines (largest gains on small models) and +7.2% over the best prior routing method while cutting route-search time 9.4x (14.8 to 1.6 hours).
board.why: It is a way to squeeze more out of a fixed open-weight model without retraining it — most valuable for small models running on constrained hardware, where a few points of accuracy for near-zero extra training cost is a real win.

board.headline: A model self-distills with no supervision
board.summary: Post-training methods that distill a model into itself ("on-policy self-distillation") usually still lean on an external signal — the correct answer, a reward from the environment, or guidance from a bigger model. U-OPSD (Unsupervised On-Policy Self-Distillation) removes all of it: it samples several of the model's own attempts, forms a pseudo-answer by majority vote when the model is confident enough (self-consistency), then teaches the model to reproduce that reasoning at the exact point in its longest wrong attempt where it first went off track. On math benchmarks (AIME24/25, HMMT25, MATH500, AMC23) it lifts Qwen3 by 8.5% and 10.7% at the 4B and 8B scales, matching or beating supervised methods (OPSD, GRPO) that use ground-truth answers.
board.why: If a model can bootstrap its own reasoning from internal consistency alone, you can improve it in domains where labelled answers are scarce or costly. The honest caveat the reader should hold onto: majority-vote self-training can also entrench mistakes the model is confidently wrong about, so gains are not guaranteed to generalize past benchmarks like these.

board.headline: Ranking-based rewards for RL reward models
board.summary: Reinforcement learning from feedback needs a reward model to score answers. The field is shifting from discriminative reward models (which emit a single number) to generative ones (which write out a comparison or judgement) — but generative reward models are good at ranking answers against each other, not at producing the lone scalar score that RL algorithms expect, so they have underdelivered in RL. RRC (Ranking-based Reward Construction) bridges the gap by deriving the reward from relative rankings: comparing a response against its own sampled peers (self-competitive) or against a small set of reference responses (anchor-guided).
board.why: It lets the stronger, more interpretable generative reward models actually drive RL training, where until now their ranking skill did not translate into a useful learning signal. Reward modelling is the quiet bottleneck of most RL-tuned assistants, so a cleaner way to wire it up compounds.

board.headline: The illusion of visual tool-use
board.summary: The "thinking-with-images" paradigm gives multimodal models active visual operations such as crop-and-zoom, on the theory that looking closer helps. This paper builds a causal test rather than trusting accuracy numbers: it intervenes at three levels — turning tool-use on or off, corrupting everything the model sees during a run, and swapping a single observation while holding the rest of the reasoning fixed — to measure whether the returned visual evidence actually causes the answer. Its metric, Visual Evidence Gain, isolates each observation's contribution. Across six models and five perception benchmarks it finds two dominant failure modes — "Calling Without Looking" (the crop has no causal effect on the answer) and "Looking Without Planning" (the crop is informative but the model schedules it incoherently) — and shows the aggregate accuracy gain is concentrated in a small "calibrated" minority of cases.
board.why: It is a caution that the headline accuracy gains from elaborate visual-tool pipelines can be an illusion — the model may be paying extra tokens for operations that do not drive its answer. A useful diagnostic to run before deploying or trusting such systems.
