board.headline: Europe wildfires force 200,000 from homes across France, Spain and Italy
board.summary: Wildfires across western France, central Spain and Italy have now forced roughly 200,000 people from their homes, authorities said Saturday 25 July, as separate blazes merged and hot, dry, windy conditions kept them out of control. In France's Gironde and Landes departments the fire drove mass evacuations around Bordeaux, while Spain - which declared its first-ever national wildfire emergency on Thursday 23 July over blazes near Madrid and in Avila - and Italy continued to battle major fires amid a Europe-wide heatwave. DW reported conditions that made it "nearly impossible for firefighters to gain the upper hand."
board.why: The evacuation total has roughly quadrupled in two days, marking one of the worst fire seasons on record for southern Europe and straining cross-border firefighting resources at peak summer.

board.headline: AMD and Anthropic strike a deal to deploy up to 2 gigawatts of MI450 GPUs for Claude
board.summary: AMD and Anthropic announced a strategic partnership under which Anthropic will deploy up to 2 gigawatts of AMD's MI450-series GPUs to train and run its Claude models. The Decoder reports the arrangement is worth up to $5 billion in AMD investment; it follows comparable AMD deals with Meta and OpenAI as the company presses its challenge to Nvidia's near-monopoly on AI accelerators. This confirms the AMD second-sourcing signal flagged as unverified in the 2026-07-21 edition — where an Anthropic move to AMD was inferred from indirect signals — with a named, on-the-record partnership.
board.why: Nvidia's dominance of training and inference silicon is the single biggest cost and supply chokepoint in the industry, and credible second-sourcing by the largest model builders is what actually erodes its pricing power over time. Anthropic committing at 2-gigawatt scale is a concrete data point that the challenge is real, not aspirational — though the "up to" framing on both the power and the dollar figure leaves the realized size open.

board.headline: US hits Switzerland with 12.5% tariff over forced-labour claims
board.summary: The US slapped a new 12.5% tariff on Swiss goods from 06:01 Swiss time on Friday 24 July, the top rate in a forced-labour trade action hitting 60 economies. The US Trade Representative, Jamieson Greer, took "final action" under Section 301 of the 1974 Trade Act — the same durable legal tool Trump used against China in his first term — imposing 10% on partners that pledged to enforce a ban on imports made with forced labour and 12.5% on those USTR judged to have "failed to adopt" such a ban; Switzerland drew the higher rate. The levies took effect at 12:01am Washington time (04:01 GMT), the moment the temporary 10% worldwide tariff — a 150-day Section 122 stopgap adopted after the Supreme Court struck down Trump's broader IEEPA tariffs in February — expired. Swiss business reaction was immediate and hostile, with employers' groups quoted calling the move "unjustified and incomprehensible," and SRF noting Switzerland comes off worse than the EU, whose separate July trade deal caps most goods at a 15% all-inclusive ceiling.
board.why: It lands a fresh, above-EU cost on Swiss exporters — pharma, machinery, watches — just as the prior tariff truce lapses, and reframes a US trade dispute as a human-rights enforcement claim against Swiss supply chains that Bern rejects.

board.headline: A dense per-step reward built to help long-horizon agents instead collapses them into a do-nothing loop
board.summary: A common recipe for teaching an agent to act over many steps is to hand it a small reward at every step for correctly predicting what it will observe next, on the theory that useful memory follows. Trained with GRPO (group-relative policy optimization — a popular RL method that scores each attempt against the average of a batch of attempts), the paper shows this recipe does not merely underperform: across Qwen3 models of three sizes on the ALFWorld household-task benchmark, it drives every run into a "dark room" — the agent maximizes prediction accuracy by doing nothing, task success falls to zero, and episodes run out the clock. A single-factor ablation pins the cause: removing only GRPO's step of dividing rewards by their standard deviation turns the same reward from catastrophic back to baseline. When every attempt in a batch fails, that division makes a bounded reward act as unbounded pressure toward the degenerate solution.
board.why: dense reward-shaping is one of the obvious levers people reach for when sparse rewards make long-horizon agents hard to train, and this is a clean, mechanistic warning that a widely used normalization step can silently convert a helpful signal into a self-inflicted collapse. The fix is two lines of code, but the lesson — that the optimizer, not the environment, built the trap — is the useful part.

board.headline: Swiss transport regulator orders cash and paper-ticket options preserved
board.summary: The Federal Office of Transport (BAV) told Switzerland's public-transport operators on Friday 24 July that they must guarantee analogue, cash-payable ticket options as machines and cash acceptance disappear. In a written directive to the industry, the BAV said every transport company must ensure that people who cannot or do not want to buy tickets digitally still have a way to obtain a valid one; spokesperson Andreas Windlinger said such passengers "should not be left behind." The rules are binding. The industry body Alliance SwissPass defended its digitalisation drive but said it would comply, pointing to existing options such as loading a ticket onto a SwissPass by phone in some regions.
board.why: It is a concrete federal check on the cashless push in daily Swiss life, protecting older passengers and those without smartphones from being locked out of the transport network.
